passage: All through Navratri, Vasudha and Sharmila had practised garba steps behind the village temple. On the fifth evening a new girl, Kamala, arrived from the city with a mirror-work skirt and quick feet. Sharmila laughed at her jokes and learned her twirl. Vasudha stood at the edge, pulling at her dupatta. When Sharmila called, "Vasu, come, Kamala's teaching us!", Vasudha said she had a headache and walked home the long way. At the gate she stopped, eyes stinging. "She'll pair with Kamala for the final night," she muttered. Next morning Sharmila turned up with two glass bangles. "One each for the last night, Vasu. You're my partner."

qa.q: What did Sharmila bring the next morning?
qa.a: She brought two glass bangles, one each for the last night.

qa.q: What was Vasudha afraid of when she walked home the long way?
qa.a: She was jealous and afraid that Sharmila would choose Kamala as her partner for the final night.

qa.q: What could Vasudha have tried instead of leaving?
qa.a: She could have joined the lesson and later told Sharmila honestly that she felt a bit left out.

qa.q: How might Sharmila have seen Vasudha's headache excuse?
qa.a: Sharmila may have sensed Vasudha was upset, which is why she came with the bangles to reassure her.

grounding: Shows a child's fear of losing her best friend to a newcomer during a festival.

passage: In the music room of their Goa school, the Christmas carol list went up on the noticeboard. "Solo: Jasleen Kaur." Maria read it twice. Jasleen, who had joined only in June, could hit the high note in the last carol without her voice cracking. Maria, who had sung in the choir since Class 2, stared at Jasleen's shiny new songbook and thought of the tattered photocopies in her own bag. At practice she sang the high note too loud, trying to be heard. Afterwards Jasleen came over. "Your harmony in the second verse is so pretty. Can you help me with it?" Maria almost said no. She said, "Okay," and felt her face go warm.

qa.q: Whose name was on the list for the solo?
qa.a: Jasleen Kaur.

qa.q: Why did Maria sing the high note too loud at practice?
qa.a: She felt envious of Jasleen's voice and solo, and wanted to be heard and noticed too.

qa.q: What could Maria do with her feelings next?
qa.a: She could accept Jasleen's request, since sharing her own strength in harmony might ease the envy and win her a friend.

qa.q: What is it like for Jasleen to ask Maria for help?
qa.a: Jasleen, new since June, seems to admire Maria's harmony and may want a friend in the choir.

grounding: Illustrates a child wanting the voice, songbook and solo that a newer classmate has.

passage: Dolma's family had moved to the hill town of Ravangla only a month before Losar. At school she ate lunch alone on the steps. The week before the new year, Irawati's group was cutting paper lanterns in the corner of the classroom. Irawati looked up. "Dolma, you know how to make the eight-point ones, right? Show us?" Dolma folded, snipped and opened a perfect star. The others crowded round. "You're in our group for the fair," Irawati declared. That evening Dolma ran all the way up the steep lane and told her Ama three times, "I'm in Irawati's group." She slept with the paper star under her pillow.

qa.q: What were Irawati's group cutting in the corner of the classroom?
qa.a: They were cutting paper lanterns.

qa.q: Why did Dolma tell her Ama three times, "I'm in Irawati's group"?
qa.a: She felt joyful and secure at last after weeks of eating alone, and the acceptance meant a great deal to her. 🤍

qa.q: How could a teacher help new students like Dolma feel included sooner?
qa.a: The teacher could set up small group tasks early and invite new students to share a skill, as Irawati did.

qa.q: What might Irawati gain by inviting Dolma?
qa.a: Irawati's group gains a skilled lantern maker, and Irawati may feel good about welcoming someone new.

grounding: Shows a new child finding deep security and happiness in being accepted by a classmates' group before a festival.

passage: Every Saturday in January the outdoor rink in Toronto was packed. Layla gripped the boards while Vera, from her class, glided backwards and spun twice with her arms tucked in. Their classmates clapped. Layla pushed away from the wall once and landed on her knees. "Everyone here learned when they were three," she mumbled to her cousin Sami, cheeks burning under her scarf. "I'm the worst in the whole class." Sami shrugged. "You've skated for two weeks." Layla watched Vera spin again and pulled her hat low. She didn't take off her skates, though. She pushed away from the boards once more.

qa.q: How many times did Vera spin?
qa.a: Vera spun twice with her arms tucked in.

qa.q: What was Layla feeling when she said she was the worst in the class?
qa.a: She felt inadequate and embarrassed, comparing her two weeks of skating with Vera's easy spins.

qa.q: What could Layla tell herself to make the comparison fairer?
qa.a: She could compare herself with her own first day, not with Vera, and notice how much she has learned in two weeks.

qa.q: How might Vera see Layla at the rink?
qa.a: Vera might not even notice Layla's struggle, or might remember learning slowly too; being judged may feel bigger to Layla than it really is.

grounding: Illustrates a child feeling inferior when she compares her new skating with a classmate's skill.

passage: It was the last day of summer sports camp at the community centre, and the relay final was close. Ira ran the third leg for her team and saw it: Tanvir, on the other team, started his run a full metre before the baton reached him. His team won by a step. Ira's face went hot. She marched to Coach Deshmukh, fists clenched. "That's cheating! He left early. Everyone saw!" Her voice cracked. Tanvir shouted, "I did not!" Coach Deshmukh raised a hand. "Let's check the video from the parents' stand." Ira stood breathing hard, arms folded, still shaking.

qa.q: Which leg did Ira run?
qa.a: She ran the third leg for her team.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when she marched to Coach Deshmukh?
qa.a: She felt angry and indignant at what looked like cheating, so strongly that her voice cracked.

qa.q: How could Ira raise the complaint so it gets heard?
qa.a: She could calmly describe exactly what she saw and let the coach check, instead of shouting that everyone saw it.

qa.q: What is it like for Tanvir to be accused in front of everyone?
qa.a: Tanvir feels attacked and defensive, whether or not he started early, so he shouts back.

grounding: Shows a child's hot reaction to what she sees as cheating in a relay race.

passage:
Dear Diary, 18 July, still raining
I was home with a cold for three days, and I was dreading Friday's maths test. This evening the doorbell rang, and it was Kavitha from my class, soaking wet, with a plastic bag. Inside were her maths notes, copied out neatly for me, with the hard sums marked in red. She must have done it after school instead of playing. I said thanks, but it didn't feel like enough. After she left I just sat there holding the pages. Tomorrow I'm going to give her my best pencil set and help her with the English poem she hates.
Kunal

qa.q: How many days was Kunal home with a cold?
qa.a: Kunal was home with a cold for three days.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel holding the pages after Kavitha left?
qa.a: Kunal felt deeply grateful and touched, knowing Kavitha had given up playtime to help. 🙏

qa.q: What could Kunal do to show thanks in a way that fits the kindness?
qa.a: Besides the pencil set, Kunal could tell Kavitha exactly how much the notes helped once the test is over.

qa.q: Why might Kavitha have come over in the rain?
qa.a: Kavitha probably cared about Kunal missing lessons and wanted to help before the Friday test.

grounding: Illustrates a child recognising and feeling thankful for a classmate's deliberate kindness during the rains.

passage:
Dear Diary, 13 August
For Independence Day our class is running a treasure hunt, and we all promised not to open the clue envelopes early. Today Mridul tried to peek at the third clue in the staffroom corridor. I said, "We promised. It's not fair on everyone else." He rolled his eyes, but four others backed me up, and he put it back. Walking home I felt about ten feet tall, like the judge in a courtroom. Then I remembered I'd almost peeked at the first clue last week myself. I'm still glad I spoke up.
Sabina

qa.q: What did Mridul try to do in the staffroom corridor?
qa.a: Mridul tried to peek at the third clue.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel walking home?
qa.a: Sabina felt proud and in the right, "about ten feet tall", for upholding the class promise.

qa.q: How could Sabina's last thought help next time?
qa.a: Remembering that almost-peek keeps the pride humble, so Sabina can speak up firmly without judging Mridul too harshly.

qa.q: How might Mridul feel after four classmates backed Sabina?
qa.a: Mridul may feel embarrassed and outnumbered, perhaps a bit resentful at being called out.

grounding: Shows a child feeling validated for upholding a rule the whole class agreed on before Independence Day.

passage: The half-yearly results came out just before the Christmas holidays at their Chennai school. Bhavna got 9 out of 25 in maths. On the bus home she stared out at the star lanterns on the balconies and didn't talk. Her cousin Charu nudged her. "You can sulk today. Tomorrow we start." That night Bhavna stuck a chart on her cupboard: twenty sums a day, every day of the holidays, ticks in green. By the tenth day she'd missed only one tick. When a hard fraction question beat her, she circled it and asked Charu in the morning instead of skipping it. "Nine was just where I started," she wrote at the top of the chart.

qa.q: What did Bhavna score in maths?
qa.a: She got 9 out of 25.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling on the bus home?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and low about her score, too upset to talk.

qa.q: What helped Bhavna keep going through the holidays?
qa.a: A small daily target with visible ticks, and asking for help with hard sums instead of skipping them, kept her effort steady.

qa.q: How does Charu help Bhavna bounce back?
qa.a: Charu allows a day to sulk but sets a firm start for tomorrow, supporting Bhavna without dismissing the disappointment.

grounding: Illustrates a child bouncing back from a poor test score with steady daily effort over the holidays.

passage: At the Baisakhi mela in their village, Amandeep bought a paper windmill and ran round until it spun. His cousin Ira grinned. "Careful, Aman, you're so full of hot air you'll take off with it." Amandeep stopped. His ears went red. "You're calling me a show-off?" Ira laughed. "No, silly. Hot air. Windmill. Get it?" Amandeep looked at the spinning paper, then at Ira's face, all crinkles, not mean at all. He snorted. "Then you're so slow you'd need a tractor to turn yours." Ira clutched her stomach laughing, and they raced to the next stall.

qa.q: What did Amandeep buy at the Baisakhi mela?
qa.a: He bought a paper windmill.

qa.q: What did Amandeep's red ears suggest at first?
qa.a: They suggest he felt hurt and embarrassed, thinking Ira was calling him a show-off.

qa.q: How did Amandeep work out that the tease wasn't mean?
qa.a: He saw the joke's link to the windmill and noticed Ira's crinkled, friendly face, then answered with a joke of his own. 😄

qa.q: What would change if Ira hadn't explained the joke?
qa.a: Amandeep might have stayed hurt, and Ira might never have known the joke had stung.

grounding: Shows a child first mistaking a cousin's pun for an insult, then getting the joke and teasing back.

passage: On Halloween night in Houston, Tuan and Diego made a deal before they set out: whatever they collected would go into one bag and be split evenly at the end. At the last house, a neighbour gave Tuan a big chocolate bar while Diego was tying his shoe. Tuan slipped it into his jacket. Walking home, the bar felt heavy. On the porch Diego counted out the sweets, one for you, one for me, careful as always. "Wait," Tuan said, and pulled out the bar. "This goes in too. We said everything." Diego broke it in half. "Next year you're my partner again."

qa.q: What did the neighbour give Tuan at the last house?
qa.a: A big chocolate bar.

qa.q: Why did the bar feel heavy to Tuan on the walk home?
qa.a: He felt guilty about breaking the deal with Diego and uneasy keeping it secret.

qa.q: Which choice kept the friendship strong, and why?
qa.a: Adding the bar to the pile kept the deal they both trusted, so Diego wants to partner again.

qa.q: How does Diego see Tuan when the bar comes out?
qa.a: Diego sees Tuan as fair and trustworthy, and rewards the honesty by asking Tuan to be a partner again next year.

grounding: Illustrates a child keeping a fair-sharing deal with a friend because they trust each other.
